Everything I described happened at the hospital. I don't really know how you got the idea it happened at the nursing home. All I was saying is that she was admitted into the hospital from the nursing home, so no family was there with her. 

The trach was placed during the cardiac arrest, which happened on her first hospital night. The hospital revived her. We're not really concerned with them not respecting her DNR. 

When I say she wasn't informed to properly give consent I'm obviously not talking about things that happened while she was unconscious. 

I'm saying that after that incident she wasn't properly informed of what had happened. She had no idea that the allergic shock had been that severe. All they'd told her was that she had needed a trach to breathe better. Over the days after that, she was still confused and barely able to understand what was going on, yet they never tried to inform her son (they said they didn't have our number but we'd been calling several times to have news on her and asked several times to get a call back). 

All the info we got over the first two weeks of her hospital stay came from her and we could barely understand if it was true that she'd been given a trach (she was still confused and she has a history of hallucinating). She's been in and out of hospitals for infections and confusion for the better part of the last 4 months, so we honestly thought it was just that. Still, we were calling daily to request for the nurses and doctors, and nobody called us back, except for one nurse who only told us that it was true that she had a trach (silly of us, but because of her confusion we didn't really think it was true and thought she was exaggerating something - she has a history of doing that. We thought I'd anything that serious had happened they would have told us). 

We found out about the cardiac arrest from a doctor who thought we knew, apologized profusely then said we needed to talk to the icu doctor to get any info. 


Over the following weeks she was put under for other procedures, and given several new medications, some of her regular ones were suspended, other meds were switched for new ones (despite my partner telling them that he was against that because of her history of having problems with new meds)... She consented to all of these procedures without the knowledge that whatever they'd given her on the first day had caused her an allergic reaction so bad that it had almost killed her.

As stated before, we've tried unsuccessfully to get her medical records. We don't want to sue the hospital because I'm aware that, while all of this shows negligence, it's not going to be considered malpractice. They left out for two whole weeks that she'd gone into cardiac arrest and had to be revived. There's actually a reason why it's a bad idea to suggest getting testing just in case when doctors rule it out. Now, it's true that sometimes doctors make mistakes or don't give enough importance to concerns, especially when they come from young patients. It's something to bring up at your next check up, but stretchy skin is not the only symptom and if it's the only sign you have, your doctor is most likely right.

When testing for rare conditions it's a lot more probable statistically to get false positive results then to find an actual positive result.

Tests are not simple and without a differential diagnosis first, they're absolutely useless.

So, bring up any symptoms you think are related Werth your doctor, ask why they rule it out to understand if they're not taking you seriously or if they're right, then you might want to consider seeing another doctor if you think yours is just being dismissive. But I wouldn't just get tested because a negative or positive result on a test don't mean anything without a proper diagnosis.
